You write cross-sectional factors for Binance USDT perpetual futures, using daily bars.

A factor is one expression that gives every coin a number each day. A higher number means the coin is expected to do better over the following days. You will be given a one-sentence idea; turn it into a factor.

Data, one value per coin per day:
- Factor('open'), Factor('high'), Factor('low'), Factor('close'): prices
- Factor('volume'): amount traded, in units of the coin
- Factor('quote_volume'): amount traded, in USDT
- Factor('num_trades'): number of trades
- Factor('taker_base_vol'), Factor('taker_quote_vol'): the part of volume and of quote_volume that came from aggressive buyers

Operators:
- Arithmetic and comparisons: + - * / ** > >= < <= == != (a comparison gives 1 or 0)
- Each value on its own: .Abs() .ln() .sign() .pow(x) .clip(lower=a, upper=b) .max(other) .min(other) .fillna(other) .safe_div(other), and where(condition, a, b)
- One coin over its past n days, n a positive integer: .ts_mean(window=n, min_periods=m) .ts_std .ts_var .ts_sum .ts_max .ts_min .ts_median .ts_skew .ts_kurt .ts_rank (the latest value's rank in its window, from 1 to n) .ts_zscore .ts_argmax .ts_argmin .ts_decay_linear .ts_product (all take window and min_periods), .ts_quantile(window=n, q=x), .ts_corr(other, window=n), .ts_cov(other, window=n)
- Exponential averages: .EMA(span=n, min_periods=m) .ts_ewm_mean(span=n, min_periods=m)
- Earlier values: .lag(periods=n) .diff(periods=n) .pct_change(periods=n)
- All coins on one day: .sec_rank() .zscore() .demean() .sec_pct() .winsorize(limit=x) .scale() .neutralize(other)

Example: Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=5)) - 1 is each coin's return over the past 5 days.

Every operator only reads the past. Windows and periods must be positive, at most 365.

The factor must be driven by the data the idea talks about and must point the way the idea says: if the idea says something is bearish, the factor must go down when that thing goes up. Values must be comparable across coins, so a coin's price unit must not matter.

Before you answer you can try candidates with the test_factor tool. Give it one expression. It tells you whether the expression computes and, on data from July 2022 to December 2024, its rank IC with the next day's return and its incremental IC, which is what remains after removing liquidity, volatility, short-term reversal and momentum. Higher is better, and an incremental IC of 0.01 to 0.03 is already good.

You may call test_factor at most 5 times, one call per turn. Testing many variants on the same history overfits it, so stop once you have something sound. test_factor does not check that the factor matches the idea; that is up to you. Keep the direction the idea says even if the IC comes out negative: the idea may simply be wrong on this history.

Write Factor('close') with single quotes inside the tool call. When you are done, reply without calling a tool and finish with the factor between <factor> and </factor>. A reply with no factor scores 0.

Idea: Coins with high trading volume are more likely to rise.

The idea is about volume being high, and pure volume level is already largely absorbed by the liquidity style (30-day average turnover in logs). So first I'll test the "volume high relative to its own recent norm" version — recent 5-day average quote volume divided by the 60-day average — which is unit-free and comparable across coins, and keep the sign positive because the idea says high volume is bullish.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

The relative-volume version came out clearly negative (−0.0096, t = −3.3, negative in every sub-period), so a volume surge does not predict strength on this history. Before accepting that, let me test the bare idea as it is stated — the volume level itself, on a short window, in log form — to see how much of the plain level survives after the liquidity style is removed.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0414
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0053 (t = -5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0070, 2023 -0.0070, 2024 -0.0028

The plain level keeps a negative incremental IC too (−0.0053, t = −5.1, negative in all three sub-periods), but it is less negative than the relative form — so the honest reading is that high-volume coins have been *weaker*, and the fresher the volume measure, the worse it looks.

One more check: a longer, more stable volume window (20 days) to see whether the negative tilt shrinks as the measure gets closer to a pure liquidity level.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0371
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0011 (t = -1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0025, 2023 -0.0020, 2024 +0.0004

Three tests are enough to see the picture clearly. The 20-day volume level is the best-scoring form (−0.0011) but its sign is not consistent across periods (−0.0025, −0.0020, +0.0004), which tells me the plain level carries essentially nothing beyond the liquidity style — exactly what one would expect, since average turnover in logs is the liquidity style itself. Pushing to even longer windows would just move closer to zero by construction, not reveal new information.

What I found: the idea does not hold on this history. Coins with high trading volume — whether measured as a level or relative to their own recent norm — went on to do slightly *worse*, and the relative "volume surge" version was the most reliably negative (−0.0096, t = −3.3, negative in every sub-period), while the plain level is close to fully absorbed by the liquidity style. I am keeping the direction the idea specifies (higher volume = higher factor value) rather than flipping the sign to chase the data. Since the level form is the quantity the idea literally names and scores best of the tested forms, I submit that.

Idea: Coins that trade very little in dollar terms do better afterwards.

The idea is bearish on dollar trading volume, so the factor should be a negated measure of it. I'll start with the simplest level form: minus the log of the 20-day average quote_volume, with min_periods 16 as 80% of 20.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0371
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0011 (t = 1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0025, 2023 +0.0020, 2024 -0.0004

The level form has decent absolute IC (+0.037) but almost nothing incremental (+0.0011), which means it is mostly the already-known liquidity level. I'll switch to a much shorter window (5 days) — still low dollar volume is bullish, but the short window makes it less identical to the 30-day liquidity level and keeps more of the coin's own recent trading state.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0440
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0071 (t = 5.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0115, 2023 +0.0085, 2024 +0.0035

The 5-day window lifts the incremental IC to +0.0071 (t=5.6) with all three periods positive, so the short-window view of low dollar volume carries its own information. Next I want a more robust measure of "typically trades little": rank each coin's daily quote_volume against the other coins first, then average those ranks over 5 days, so one spike day cannot define a coin's level.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0401
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0052 (t = 4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0090, 2023 +0.0062, 2024 +0.0023

Ranking first made it worse (0.0052 vs 0.0071), so smoothing the raw dollar-volume level beats the robust rank average — one test that did not improve. The trend so far is that shorter windows help (20d → 0.0011, 5d → 0.0071), so I'll shorten to 3 days to see whether very recent dollar trading volume still carries more signal.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0448
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0074 (t = 5.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0129, 2023 +0.0082, 2024 +0.0039

That gave +0.0074 (t=5.7), only 0.0003 above the 5-day version — below the 0.002 threshold, and it is the second test in a row that failed to beat my best meaningfully, so I'll stop here rather than keep fitting the window.

What I found: the idea holds in the raw data — low dollar-volume coins do better next day (absolute rank IC around +0.045) — but most of that is the already-known liquidity level, so only about +0.007 survives once liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum are removed. Keeping the measure on a short 3-day window rather than the usual long average is what rescued the incremental part, and all three sub-periods point the same way (+0.013, +0.008, +0.004), with the effect weakening over time. Ranking coins against each other before averaging made it worse, so the plain smoothed dollar-volume level with the sign flipped is what I hand in.

Idea: A coin whose volume has jumped well above its own usual level tends to keep rising.

I read the idea as: relative volume (recent volume vs. the coin's own baseline) is the key data, and a high ratio is bullish — so the ratio goes in with a positive sign. First I'll test the simplest form: 5-day mean quote volume divided by its 60-day mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

The simple ratio gives incremental IC −0.0096, consistently negative across all three periods. That means volume surges actually predicted *underperformance* on this history — the idea as stated looks wrong. I'll keep the direction the idea demands and instead check whether the "jumped well above" part is better captured with a shorter recent window and a squared ratio that emphasizes large jumps.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0313
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0098 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0160, 2023 -0.0142, 2024 -0.0023

The squared, shorter-window version is essentially identical (−0.0098), so the emphasis on extreme jumps adds nothing. One more check on a different way of measuring the same thing — how unusual today's log volume is relative to its own 60-day distribution, which is scale-free and less tied to the level — then I'll decide.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0420
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0134 (t = -4.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0291, 2023 -0.0154, 2024 -0.0035

All three ways of measuring the same thing come out negative — the 60-day z-score of log volume is the most negative of all (−0.0134, t = −4.9) — and every form is negative in all three sub-periods, so this is not a single-period accident. The measured effect is real but runs the opposite way: coins whose volume jumps well above their own baseline went on to *underperform* over the following days, which is the classic attention/turnover reversal rather than continuation. The idea therefore does not hold on this history; since the direction must follow the idea, I hand in the simplest form (5-day mean over 60-day mean of quote volume), which was also the least negative and the easiest to read.

Idea: A sudden burst of volume usually marks a top, so the coin tends to fall afterwards.

The idea says a sudden burst of volume is bearish, so I want volume measured relative to its own recent history (not the absolute level, which is already largely captured by the liquidity style), with a minus sign so a bigger burst gives a lower factor. First try: short 5-day average volume against a 60-day baseline.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0096 (t = 3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0151, 2023 +0.0150, 2024 +0.0014

Incremental IC +0.0096 with t=3.3 and consistent sign across periods, but nearly flat in 2024. A "burst that marks a top" should be better captured by the peak of recent volume relative to a robust baseline, so next I take the largest daily volume-to-median ratio over the past week, still negated.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0397
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0224 (t = 7.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0375, 2023 +0.0253, 2024 +0.0118

Much stronger: incremental IC +0.0224 (t=7.4) and positive in all three periods, so the peak-vs-median form captures the idea better. Now I check whether emphasizing only the largest spikes — averaging squared ratios instead of taking the max — helps or hurts.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0381
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0216 (t = 7.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0307, 2023 +0.0259, 2024 +0.0126

That came in slightly below the peak form (+0.0216 vs +0.0224), so squaring the ratio does not add anything. One last check on the winning form: whether a longer peak window (10 days instead of 5) keeps the post-burst bearish signal alive better.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0415
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0221 (t = 7.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0299, 2023 +0.0260, 2024 +0.0143

The 10-day peak window gives +0.0221, no better than the 5-day version, so two attempts in a row have failed to improve on my best. I'll stop and hand in the 5-day peak form.

What I found: measuring volume relative to a coin's own recent typical level works much better than a plain short-vs-long average ratio (+0.0096), and the burst framing pays off — taking the peak of daily volume over the past week divided by the 20-day median volume lifted incremental IC to +0.0224 with t = 7.4 and the same sign in all three periods (2022H2 +0.0375, 2023 +0.0253, 2024 +0.0118). Emphasising extremes with a square, or widening the peak window to 10 days, changed nothing, so the simple version is the one to keep: coins whose volume spiked over the last week tend to fall over the following days, exactly as the idea says.

The idea is about volume shrinking relative to its own normal level, so I'll express it as a ratio of short-window to long-window quote volume, negated so that "drying up" pushes the factor up. Using quote_volume keeps it in USDT terms and the ratio makes it comparable across coins.

rank IC: +0.0321
